idiom_name: interface{ Update(dt float64) } in a slice walked with range
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance, so the abstract hook becomes a one-method interface satisfied implicitly by any type with that method, the collection is a slice, and the driver is a range loop - there is no base class or entity manager to write. What replaces the classic structure: the interface replaces the abstract update hook (pointer receivers are required for mutation) and the slice plus range replaces the manager, which is enough because Go's interfaces already dispatch dynamically; the classic structure is not missed. With Ebitengine the frame belongs to the engine ('Update is called every tick (1/60 [s] by default)'), so you walk your own entities inside the single Game.Update rather than driving the loop yourself.
pitfalls: range copies the slice header at entry, so appended entities are not stepped this frame (usually intended, but it must be a decision), and deleting with append(s[:i], s[i+1:]...) shifts the tail so the next element is skipped.
Mutation needs pointer receivers or a slice of pointers: a value receiver's Update mutates a copy and the entity appears frozen.
A nil interface value panics when called, so guard skipped entries or keep a separate live-entity slice.
Sharing the entity slice between goroutines turns every step into a data race; partition the slice per worker or serialise, and keep cross-object effects out of the walk.
